authoredPrompt: This figure looks straight down the axis of a chair-form cyclohexane ring in two matched models that color-code the two kinds of hydrogen position. On the left is a space-filling model: a compact dark gray core of ring carbons is surrounded by six large red spheres and six large blue spheres packed against one another, the red ones sitting toward the center of the disc and the blue ones fanning outward around the rim, the two colors alternating as the eye travels around the ring. A magenta arrow at the upper left points to a red sphere and is labeled "Axial"; a blue arrow at the top points to a blue sphere and is labeled "Equatorial". On the right the same view appears as a ball-and-stick model, the six dark gray carbons forming a hexagonal outline, with red spheres projecting from alternating carbons and blue spheres held outward from every carbon on thin pale rods. Separating the two positions by color rather than by perspective lets the reader count them directly, establishing that each ring carbon bears exactly one axial and one equatorial hydrogen and that each face carries three of each in alternating order.
authoredInteractions:
- Click for selecting any ring carbon in the ball-and-stick model; its paired axial and equatorial hydrogens brighten together, clarifying that the two positions coexist on each carbon rather than belonging to separate molecules.
- Toggle axial only, equatorial only, and both: red and blue hydrogens fade in and out on both models, making the one-axial-one-equatorial pattern at every ring carbon countable.
authoredContext:
As shown in the figure, each carbon atom in chair cyclohexane has one axial and one equatorial hydrogen. Furthermore, each side of the ring has three axial and three equatorial hydrogens in an alternating arrangement. For example, if the top side of the ring has axial hydrogens on carbons 1, 3, and 5, then it has equatorial hydrogens on carbons 2, 4, and 6. The reverse is true for the bottom side: carbons 1, 3, and 5 have equatorial hydrogens, but carbons 2, 4, and 6 have axial hydrogens (the figure).

Alternating axial and equatorial positions in chair cyclohexane, looking directly down the ring axis. Each carbon atom has one axial and one equatorial position, and each face has alternating axial and equatorial positions.

The space-filling model and ball and stick model of cyclohexane with alternate axial and equatorial positions, represented by red and blue spheres, respectively.

Note that we haven’t used the words cis and trans in this discussion of cyclohexane conformation. Two hydrogens on the same side of the ring are always cis, regardless of whether they’re axial or equatorial and regardless of whether they’re adjacent. Similarly, two hydrogens on opposite sides of the ring are always trans.

evaluation.notes: The concept of axial vs equatorial hydrogens is correctly encoded and the toggle interaction is pedagogically useful, but the vertical stacking layout and near-top-down camera angle destroy the recognizable side-by-side composition and 3D chair structure of the source figure.
action_items: Change camera elevation from 88° to approximately 15-25° to show the 3D chair conformation with visible up/down carbon alternation
Arrange the two models side-by-side (space-filling at x=-1.7, ball-and-stick at x=+1.7) with a front-facing camera rather than stacking them vertically
Increase label font size to at least 20px and reposition labels outside the model with longer arrows pointing to specific atoms
Make space-filling spheres larger relative to carbon spheres so they overlap and hide the carbons, matching the compact appearance of the source
plan_action_items: The plan should specify a low-elevation camera angle (10-25°) to preserve the 3D chair structure, and a horizontal side-by-side layout matching the source composition
